osaka_sushi_hamuro.notes: [Sushi · a six-seat alley counter off Shinsaibashi-suji] A six-seat sushi counter at the end of a narrow alley, where only the sign shows from the street. It's been open since 2015, and the owner has thirty years of experience. The meal is an omakase of seasonal fish, sushi and small dishes, and you can add favorites. Diners remember the kohada (one called it the best ever), sweet red sea urchin, nodoguro, katsuo tataki, crab, and winter fugu milt. It finishes with ushiojiru. The chef pairs sake to the food. The owner is gentle and the room calm, and regulars keep it full; reservations are hard to get. Courses are good value, drinks less so. Reviewers spent about ¥10,000–30,000.

chef_bio.background: Owner with 30 years of experience (April 2024 review).

osaka_misono_hozenji.notes: [Japanese · a chicken specialist beside Hōzenji] A chicken restaurant in the building next to Mizukake Fudō, cooking domestically raised young chickens from sashimi to rice. The assorted chicken sashimi is fresh and bouncy, the thigh tataki hits hard with garlic, and the kara-age, especially the crisp wings, is a favorite; one diner ordered four plates of grilled cartilage. Look also for fried chicken skin rolled with green onion, liver, gizzards and a spicy simmered chicken skin to eat over rice. Courses run to mizutaki, refined in chicken flavor, with rice porridge, and there is a dry curry omurice. Service is quiet but kind, with plates split for groups. Seats fill within minutes, so reserve. Sake is limited; beer and shochu are there.

chef_bio.background: Chicken specialist using domestically raised young chickens; official site tori-misono.com (Tabelog).

Also on the board: thigh tataki, gizzard, red sausage, a spicy yam kimchi, smashed cucumber, and a chazuke in chicken broth to finish. It's a proper old-school local joint. One diner waited a while for orders. Only six seats, so call ahead. Open until 3 am; closed Sundays. Cash only.

osaka_yakiniku_p_takanosuke.notes: [Yakiniku · a six-seat alley counter where the master grills] A hidden yakiniku counter in a narrow Souemoncho alley, next door to Hiromiya. There are no grills at the seats: the master grills each cut and serves it at its best, so up to about seven diners squeeze in close. Portions are about half the usual size, so you can try many cuts. Start with white senmai, when there is any, with sesame oil, salt and a moreish miso. Then go to aburi yukke, wagyu tataki, salted tongue, outside skirt and kalbi. A Korean-style cold tofu with kimchi and seaweed is a side. It's easy to drop by alone, and the owner suits the room. Open late, to 2 am. Cash only; smoking allowed.

osaka_ikareta_noodle_fish_tons.notes: [Ramen · Shinmachi's Ramen 100 seafood-tonkotsu tsukemen] A tsukemen shop near Nishi-Ohashi, open since 2017 and picked for Tabelog's Ramen OSAKA 100 in 2023, 2024 and 2025. The dipping sauce is thick pork bone and seafood, bonito-forward, and it clings to homemade thick, flat noodles chilled in water for a chewy, wheaty bite. Add diced onion and aji daikon as you go, then finish with soup or Dive Rice, a small bowl of rice with green onion to drop into the sauce. The TOKYO-X premium tsukemen (¥1,500) carries juicy rare chashu. There's also a seafood tonkotsu ramen (¥1,000) with a free large size. On Saturdays there is a 7 am morning ramen, such as a charcoal-grilled chashu miso. Noodles were too soft for one pair. Expect a short line at lunch. House rules: one bowl each, no phones while eating.

osaka_seimenya_nipponbashi.notes: [Ramen · a two-person tsukemen shop at the south end of Otaroad] A 13-seat noodle shop at the southern tip of Nipponbashi's Otaroad, open since 2013 and run by two: a chef in the kitchen and one person serving, both notably polite. The draw is chicken-shoyu tsukemen (¥1,330 for medium): smooth, glossy noodles and a gentle soy dipping sauce full of chicken, with tenkasu and black shichimi, mild enough to drink on its own. There's also chicken paitan on medium-thick curly noodles; this autumn it carried a curry ball you break into the broth. In summer the chilled niboshi soba (¥1,250) comes with a rice to drown in the cold broth. One bowl took about 15 minutes. Lunch only; closed Tuesdays.

osaka_kawachiriba_minamisenba.notes: [Ramen · clam-broth chuka soba for lunch near Nagahoribashi] An eight-seat lunch counter near Nagahoribashi, open since 2021, built on a clear shellfish broth. The kaidashi shio ramen tastes most clearly of clam, light yet deep. The asari shoyu is lighter still, too subtle for some, and the shichimi from Sakai's Yamatsu Tsujita lifts it. Smooth, chewy noodles are the constant praise; one diner ordered extra noodles. Thin chashu, seasoned egg and menma complete the bowl, and the shio set adds rice with clam tsukudani; sansho on the counter suits it. There's also a meat soba, and it once served cold pasta. A calm room with many women dining. Lunch only, Monday to Saturday. Cash only.

chef_bio.background: Clam-broth chuka soba, lunch only (Tabelog, staff-maintained).

In between come a liver pâté that won over one liver skeptic, a chicken-broth chawanmushi and homemade pickles. Finish with yakitori don, grilled rice-ball soup or soboro don. À la carte works too. Reserve; closed Wednesdays.

osaka_ramen_r_namba.notes: [Ramen · a big Jiro-style shop open all night near Ebisucho] A large, clean Jiro-inspired ramen shop between Ebisucho and Namba, open since 2022, with 27 seats including tables. Noodles and broth are made in-house: flat, wavy noodles of Maturité flour that one diner found dense and packed with wheat. A bowl (¥1,200 in October 2026) comes with 100 g to 300 g of noodles for the same price; call your vegetables and fat, and add garlic yourself. Expect a fatty, heavy broth and thick chashu; one diner found the soup too sour, another the pork underheated. There is also R's set meal (¥1,000), which one diner had on a weekend morning: bean sprouts, thick chashu and a fried egg with rice, tonkotsu soup and kimchi. Open 24 hours Saturday to Monday and until 04:00 most other nights. Cash only.

osaka_men_to_mugen_no_kanosei_honmachi.notes: [Ramen · Jiro-style mazesoba and a light scallop paitan by Honmachi] A tiny seven-seat counter near Honmachi, open since March 2025 and named as the brand's head shop. The mazesoba (¥1,050) is the draw: thick, chewy, wheaty noodles in a rich sauce with crunchy bean sprouts, onion and crispy garlic chips. Add chopped garlic from the counter, as it can taste flat without, and vinegar near the end; the spicy version (¥1,150, large 300 g) adds plenty of back fat, rare chashu and fried onion. In summer there is a chilled soupless Jiro-style ramen. The chicken paitan (¥950) is the opposite: light and smooth, with scallop broth, chunks of scallop, curly egg noodles and big menma; one diner found it only average. Extra rice is ¥50. Some nights there is a 10-minute wait.

osaka_sakanaya_kojun_shinsaibashi.notes: [Japanese · a fish-led izakaya and sake bar run by two off Shinsaibashi-suji] A hidden counter izakaya at the back of a building's ground-floor arcade, open since 2019 and run by two. The owner is a cook of Japanese cuisine and a sommelier, so it suits both sake and wine drinkers: sake from around Japan rotates, and wine is chosen to match what you eat. Fish comes first, with sashimi from the morning's buying, but the menu wanders: the signature, per the shop and one weekly regular, is the keema curry dashimaki (house keema rolled into egg), alongside chicken tempura with tartar, potato salad, salted sweet-potato tempura and sansho rice balls with red miso soup to finish. Seasonal set courses are available by advance booking; one December 2025 course included abalone chawanmushi and an assorted sashimi platter. One regular praises the pacing and attentive but unintrusive service. Book counter seats online; closed Tuesdays.

osaka_ranpuya_shinsaibashi.notes: [Japanese · a one-person basement kushikatsu counter on Shinsaibashi-suji] An eight-seat counter down a flight of stairs off the Shinsaibashi-suji arcade, run single-handedly; one diner felt most customers were regulars. Kushikatsu are fried to order and handed over one at a time, so each is crisp; the batter is thin enough that the ingredient shows through, and one diner found not a single miss. Beyond the usual sauce you can dip in shrimp salt or lemon soy. One diner recommends the kelp with roe and the shrimp bread (ebi pan), and another ended with a shrimp-salt rice ball. Portions are small, so you can try many. It's homey: take drinks from the fridge yourself and write down your order. With one person cooking it can feel busy. Book ahead; it fills up. Smoking allowed.

chef_bio.background: Kushikatsu counter run by one person (2024–2026 reviews; Tabelog, staff-maintained).

anecdotes.text: "The kushikatsu is fried right after you order, and each skewer is served one by one, ensuring they are all crispy. The batter is perfectly thin, allowing the flavors of the ingredients to shine through without feeling heavy." — August 2025.

"You can grab drinks from the refrigerator yourself, and you place your orders by writing them down, giving it a very homey feeling… I highly recommend the kombu kelp with roe and the shrimp bread." — November 2024.

osaka_bar_kawana_hozenji.notes: [Bar · a hidden wood-rich bar up a staircase by Hozenji] A classic bar you would walk past: in a narrow alley near Hozenji, a barely-marked steep staircase leads to a second door and then a warm, wood-rich room with records playing, a counter and a table in back. One reviewer notes that charred marks from a 2002 fire still show on the counter. The drinks list is short but well made: fresh-fruit cocktails squeezed to order, gin and tonic, a short cocktail left to the bartender, whisky such as Bowmore. Snacks are nuts and dried fruit; one diner loved the dried orange slices. Diners describe the master as easygoing and easy to talk to, and it's calm despite Hozenji Yokocho next door, with overseas visitors among the customers. A seat charge applied (about ¥1,000 in 2024); six drinks for two came to ¥7,500 in February 2026. Non-smoking. Mind the stairs.

chef_bio.background: Bar near Hozenji (2024–2026 reviews).

osaka_sea_station_dotonbori.notes: [Japanese · a fresh-fish izakaya bar over the Dotonbori canal] A fourth-floor izakaya bar right by Dotonbori Bridge, open since 2011, whose windows look out on the canal; the four-seat sofa by the window is the spot. The menu runs to 60-plus dishes with Okinawan touches, and an eel rice ball makes a filling finish. Drinks are the other draw, with 200-plus choices, including over 100 sakes a year, which the manager will suggest, plus a good shochu list. The master is friendly. Courses with all-you-can-drink suit groups, up to 30 for private hire. A ¥550 appetizer charge applies; one diner found the billing unclear. Cash only; smoking allowed.

osaka_chuka_soba_kazura_awaza.notes: [Ramen · a Tabelog 100 frothy chicken dashi soba for under ¥700] A nine-seat counter a minute from Honmachi exit 23, open since 2015 and picked for Tabelog's Ramen OSAKA 100 in 2023, 2024 and 2025, famous for big quality at a small price. The dashi soba (¥690 in October 2026) is a foamy, espuma-style chicken paitan with katsuobushi; one diner found bonito flakes settled at the bottom and stirred them in. It's creamy yet not heavy, seasoned with Aichi soy sauces. House-made medium straight noodles are smooth and chewy, and the chashu and egg have a smoky edge. Premium toppings add extra chashu and a seasoned egg for ¥150; a cold soba with roast-pork rice bowl comes in under ¥1,000. Diners report lines of five to eight and 10- to 15-minute waits at lunch, with chairs outside; bowls arrive in about five minutes, and rice can sell out. Lunch only; closed Fridays.

Bowls are thick noodles (150 g to 400 g) under a mountain of crunchy bean sprouts in a rich soy-based pork broth sweet with back fat, piping hot to the end; call your garlic, vegetables and fat, or go "everything extra". There's also a dry ramen, plus toppings like double pork, cheese and egg. The staff are the other draw: energetic, patient with first-timers and cheering you on, but there's a strict no-leftovers policy, so order honestly. Closed Sundays.

The room is dark and stylish, with counter, tables and sofas, roomy for a tsukemen shop. The signature spicy tsukemen (¥1,000, level 1 to 3) has a thick red dip of pork bone and dried mackerel blended with miso, chilies, chili oil and shrimp, nicely balanced between seafood and heat, and it stays warm. Noodles are medium-thick and chewy, 200 g or 300 g, with thick pork-belly chashu and a seasoned egg; finish with the yuzu soup. The ajitama tsukemen is the classic, and one diner had the hot-noodle version for ¥950. Grilled gyoza on the side. Buy a ticket at the door. Cash only; open daily.
